questions.stem: Who is regarded as the 'Father of Evolution' for proposing natural selection as the mechanism of evolution?
options: Gregor Mendel
Charles Darwin
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
Alfred Russel Wallace
questions.explanation: Charles Darwin (1809–1882) is regarded as the Father of Evolution. His book 'On the Origin of Species' (1859) proposed natural selection as the mechanism by which species evolve. Alfred Russel Wallace independently arrived at similar conclusions and their joint paper was presented in 1858, but Darwin's name is more closely associated. Lamarck proposed an earlier (incorrect) theory of inheritance of acquired characters.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The book 'On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection' was published in:
questions.explanation: Charles Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species' on 24 November 1859. The book sold out on its first day. It introduced two key concepts: descent with modification (common ancestry) and natural selection (the mechanism). 1809 was Darwin's birth year. The book revolutionised biology and remains one of the most important scientific works ever written.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Lamarck's theory of evolution is best summarised as:
options: Survival of the fittest
Inheritance of acquired characteristics
Gradual change by random mutation
Punctuated equilibrium
questions.explanation: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck (1744–1829) proposed that traits acquired during an organism's lifetime (e.g., a giraffe's longer neck from stretching) could be passed to offspring. This was disproved by August Weismann (mice tail-cutting experiment) and later by genetics (acquired changes don't alter germ cells). 'Survival of the fittest' is Darwinian; punctuated equilibrium is by Eldredge and Gould.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The famous finches studied by Darwin on his voyage on HMS Beagle were found on which islands?
options: Hawaiian Islands
Galapagos Islands
Falkland Islands
Canary Islands
questions.explanation: Darwin observed 13 closely-related finch species on the Galapagos Islands (off Ecuador) during the HMS Beagle voyage (1831–1836). Each species had a beak shape adapted to its food source — seed crackers, insect catchers, cactus feeders. This adaptive radiation became a cornerstone example of natural selection. They are now called 'Darwin's finches'.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Homologous organs are organs that have:
options: Different structure but similar function (e.g. wings of bird and insect)
Similar embryonic origin and structure but possibly different functions (e.g. forelimb of human, whale, bat)
No common ancestry and no functional similarity
Lost function but retain structure (vestigial)
questions.explanation: Homologous organs share a common evolutionary origin — same basic structure and embryonic development — even if functions differ. Examples: forelimb of human (grasping), whale (swimming), bat (flying), horse (running). All have the same bone arrangement (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals). Analogous organs (option A) have similar function but different origin. Vestigial organs (option D) are reduced/non-functional remnants.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: An example of analogous organs (different evolutionary origin, similar function) is:
options: Forelimb of human and wing of bat
Wings of butterfly and wings of bird
Eye of human and eye of octopus
Both B and C are correct examples
questions.explanation: Both options B and C are correct: (B) Wings of butterfly (chitinous membrane) and wings of bird (modified forelimb) evolved independently to enable flight — different structures, same function. (C) Eyes of vertebrates and octopuses both have a lens-retina system but evolved separately. These are classic examples of convergent evolution producing analogous structures. Option A is HOMOLOGOUS (shared origin).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Vestigial organs in humans include:
options: Heart, kidney, liver
Appendix, wisdom teeth, coccyx (tailbone), ear muscles
Brain, lungs, stomach
Eyes, ears, nose
questions.explanation: Vestigial organs are reduced or non-functional remnants of structures that were functional in ancestors. In humans: appendix (digesting cellulose in ancestral herbivores), wisdom teeth (larger jaws ago), coccyx (lost tail), nictitating membrane (third eyelid in plica semilunaris), goosebumps (ancestral fur erection), ear-wiggling muscles, and male nipples. About 100+ vestigial structures are documented in humans, providing strong evidence of evolution.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Genetic drift differs from natural selection in that:
options: Genetic drift acts only on dominant alleles; natural selection acts on recessive alleles
Genetic drift involves random changes in allele frequency, whereas natural selection involves non-random differential survival/reproduction based on fitness
Genetic drift is faster than natural selection in all populations
Genetic drift only occurs in plants; natural selection only in animals
questions.explanation: Genetic drift is the random change in allele frequencies due to chance — particularly significant in small populations. Natural selection is non-random: alleles that increase fitness become more common, those decreasing fitness become rarer. Bottleneck effect (population crash) and founder effect (small group colonising new area) are special cases of genetic drift. Both are mechanisms of evolution but only natural selection is adaptive.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The 'Industrial Melanism' phenomenon observed in peppered moths (Biston betularia) in 19th-century England is a textbook example of:
options: Lamarckian inheritance of acquired characteristics
Natural selection in action over a few generations as dark-coloured forms became advantageous on soot-blackened tree bark
Genetic drift caused by random pollution-induced mutations
Convergent evolution between moths and beetles
questions.explanation: Before the Industrial Revolution, light-coloured peppered moths were common (camouflaged on lichen-covered tree bark). Industrial soot killed lichens and darkened bark. The rare dark (melanic) form became less visible to bird predators, and within decades the dark form dominated industrial areas. After clean-air legislation, light forms rebounded. This is a textbook example of natural selection observed within human lifetimes. Documented by H.B.D. Kettlewell.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The Hardy-Weinberg principle in population genetics states that in the ABSENCE of evolutionary forces, allele frequencies in a population:
options: Drift randomly over time
Remain constant from generation to generation
Shift toward dominant alleles
Shift toward fitter alleles
questions.explanation: The Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (1908) states that allele and genotype frequencies remain constant across generations IF there is: no mutation, no migration, no genetic drift (infinite population size), no natural selection, and random mating. Deviation from H-W equilibrium indicates evolution is occurring. The equation p² + 2pq + q² = 1 lets us calculate allele frequencies. It serves as the null model in population genetics.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: A.I. Oparin and J.B.S. Haldane (independently in the 1920s) proposed which theory about the origin of life on Earth?
options: Life was brought to Earth by meteorites (panspermia)
Life originated from a 'primordial soup' of organic molecules formed in Earth's early reducing atmosphere
Life was created by divine intervention 6,000 years ago
Life originated in deep-sea hydrothermal vents (extremophile theory)
questions.explanation: The Oparin-Haldane hypothesis (1924, 1929) proposed that early Earth had a reducing atmosphere (rich in methane, ammonia, water vapor, hydrogen), and energy sources (lightning, UV, volcanic heat) drove the formation of organic molecules in the early oceans — the 'primordial soup'. These molecules eventually self-organized into proto-cells. The Miller-Urey experiment (1953) provided experimental support by synthesizing amino acids from these conditions.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The Miller-Urey experiment (1953) is significant because it:
options: Disproved the Oparin-Haldane hypothesis
Demonstrated that organic molecules (including amino acids) could form spontaneously under simulated primitive Earth conditions
Proved that life originated in outer space and arrived via meteorites
Showed that DNA replication can occur without enzymes
questions.explanation: Stanley Miller and Harold Urey at the University of Chicago (1953) created a closed apparatus simulating early Earth: a 'primordial' atmosphere (methane, ammonia, water vapour, hydrogen), 'oceans' (boiling water), and 'lightning' (electric sparks). After running for a week, they detected amino acids — the building blocks of proteins. This experiment provided crucial support for the Oparin-Haldane hypothesis on abiogenesis.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Speciation by geographic isolation, in which a single population is physically separated by a barrier (mountains, rivers, ocean) into two populations that diverge into different species, is called:
options: Sympatric speciation
Allopatric speciation
Peripatric speciation
Parapatric speciation
questions.explanation: Allopatric speciation (from Greek 'other place') is the most common mode of speciation. A physical barrier divides a population — for example, the Isthmus of Panama splitting Atlantic and Pacific shrimp populations. Over generations, the separated populations accumulate genetic differences and may become reproductively isolated. Sympatric (same place) speciation occurs without geographic isolation; peripatric involves a small isolated founder population; parapatric involves adjacent populations with limited gene flow.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly orders the major divisions of geological/biological history from earliest to latest?
options: Mesozoic → Paleozoic → Cenozoic
Paleozoic → Cenozoic → Mesozoic
Paleozoic → Mesozoic → Cenozoic
Cenozoic → Mesozoic → Paleozoic
questions.explanation: Phanerozoic Eon is divided into three Eras in order: (1) Paleozoic (541–252 mya) — 'ancient life', includes Cambrian explosion, fish, amphibians, reptiles; ended with Permian-Triassic extinction; (2) Mesozoic (252–66 mya) — 'middle life', the Age of Dinosaurs, includes Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous; ended with K-T extinction; (3) Cenozoic (66 mya–present) — 'recent life', Age of Mammals.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The mass extinction that ended the Cretaceous period (~66 million years ago) and wiped out non-avian dinosaurs is most strongly attributed to:
options: A large asteroid impact at Chicxulub (modern Yucatán, Mexico) that caused 'impact winter', combined with massive Deccan Traps volcanic activity in present-day India
Gradual climate cooling over millions of years that the dinosaurs couldn't adapt to
A mass disease outbreak among reptiles
Sea-level changes alone
questions.explanation: The K-Pg (Cretaceous-Paleogene) extinction was caused primarily by a ~10-15 km asteroid impact at Chicxulub (Yucatán, Mexico) that ejected dust and aerosols blocking sunlight, causing months of cold and ecosystem collapse. The Deccan Traps volcanic eruptions in India (covering ~500,000 km²) contributed additional stress. This combination caused ~75% of species, including non-avian dinosaurs, to go extinct. Mammals and birds survived.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The genus Homo (humans and direct ancestors) emerged approximately how long ago?
options: 50,000 years ago
500,000 years ago
2.5 million years ago
65 million years ago
questions.explanation: The genus Homo emerged approximately 2.5 million years ago in Africa, with Homo habilis ('handy man') being one of the earliest species. Modern Homo sapiens evolved about 300,000 years ago. The split between humans and chimpanzees was about 6-7 million years ago. Australopithecus (e.g., 'Lucy', ~3.2 mya) was a pre-Homo hominin. Option D (65 mya) is when mammals diversified after the dinosaur extinction.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Convergent evolution refers to:
options: Two unrelated species independently evolving similar traits to adapt to similar environments (e.g. dolphins and ichthyosaurs both became streamlined swimmers)
A single species splitting into many forms (adaptive radiation)
Closely-related species evolving very different traits (divergent evolution)
Hybridization between two species
questions.explanation: Convergent evolution: unrelated species facing similar selective pressures evolve similar adaptations. Classic examples: dolphins (mammals) and ichthyosaurs (extinct marine reptiles) both have streamlined fish-like bodies for aquatic life; bird wings and bat wings serve the same function via different structures. The opposite is divergent evolution where related species diverge (Darwin's finches). Adaptive radiation is when one species rapidly diversifies into multiple niches.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Which of the following provides the STRONGEST direct evidence for evolution?
options: Fossil record showing transitional forms (e.g., Archaeopteryx between reptiles and birds; Tiktaalik between fish and tetrapods)
Comparative anatomy alone (homologous organs)
Embryonic similarity (von Baer's law)
Geographic distribution of species (biogeography)
questions.explanation: All four are valid lines of evidence, but transitional fossils provide the most direct, time-stamped evidence: Archaeopteryx (~150 mya) shows reptilian features (teeth, bony tail) combined with feathers — clear intermediate between dinosaurs and birds. Tiktaalik roseae (~375 mya) shows fish features combined with tetrapod-like limbs. Comparative anatomy, embryology, and biogeography are powerful supporting evidence but transitional fossils document evolution in physical specimens.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Coevolution is best described as:
options: A species evolving twice — once forward, once backward
Two species evolving together with reciprocal influence on each other (e.g. flowers and pollinators; predators and prey; hosts and parasites)
Multiple species evolving from a common ancestor
Convergent evolution at the population level
questions.explanation: Coevolution: two species exert reciprocal selective pressures on each other and evolve in response. Classic examples: (a) flowering plants and their pollinators (corolla shape ↔ insect proboscis length); (b) predator-prey arms races (cheetahs ↔ gazelles); (c) hosts and parasites (immune systems ↔ pathogen evasion); (d) mutualistic relationships (acacia trees ↔ ants). Coevolution drives much of biological diversity.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The 'Cambrian explosion' (~540 million years ago) refers to:
options: The first appearance of life on Earth
A relatively rapid (geologically speaking) diversification of multicellular animal phyla in the early Cambrian period
The mass extinction at the end of the Cambrian period
A volcanic eruption that created the Cambrian mountain range
questions.explanation: The Cambrian explosion (~541-530 mya) was a remarkable, geologically rapid (over ~20 million years) appearance of most major animal phyla in the fossil record. Before this, life was mostly simple/microscopic; suddenly we see complex multicellular organisms with hard parts (shells, exoskeletons). The Burgess Shale fossils document this diversification. Causes are debated: rising oxygen levels, predator-prey arms races, evolution of vision, and the development of Hox genes are all candidates.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Punctuated equilibrium (Eldredge & Gould, 1972) differs from Darwinian gradualism in proposing that:
options: Species change continuously at a steady, gradual rate across their entire history
Species exist mostly in long periods of evolutionary stasis interrupted by short bursts of rapid change (often during speciation events)
Evolution doesn't occur — species are immutable
Major evolutionary change happens only at the individual level, not the species level
questions.explanation: Punctuated equilibrium proposes that fossil records show species remaining largely unchanged for long periods (stasis, often millions of years), then undergoing relatively rapid changes (geologically — tens of thousands of years) during speciation events. This contrasts with the gradualist view that species change continuously and steadily. The two views aren't mutually exclusive — both modes of evolution occur, and modern theory accommodates both patterns.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: An island has 10,000 people of which 1% have a recessive autosomal disorder (qq). Using the Hardy-Weinberg principle, what percentage of the population are CARRIERS (heterozygous, Qq) of this disorder?
questions.explanation: Given q² = 0.01 (1% affected), so q = 0.1, p = 0.9. Carrier frequency = 2pq = 2 × 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.18 = 18%. **Short Trick:** If q² = 0.01, then q = √0.01 = 0.1; p = 1 - q = 0.9; carriers (Qq) = 2pq = 2 × 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.18 = 18%. So while only 1% express the disease, nearly 1 in 5 are unaffected carriers — a common situation that surprises students.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The Modern Synthesis (Modern Evolutionary Synthesis), developed in the 1930s–1940s, unified Darwinian evolution with which other field?
options: Mendelian genetics — combining natural selection with population genetics, work of Fisher, Haldane, Wright, Dobzhansky, Mayr, and Simpson
Behavioral psychology
Quantum mechanics
Cell biology only, without incorporating genetics
questions.explanation: The Modern Synthesis (1930s-1940s) integrated Darwinian natural selection with Mendelian genetics, population genetics, and paleontology. Key contributors: R.A. Fisher, J.B.S. Haldane, Sewall Wright (population genetics theory); Theodosius Dobzhansky ('Genetics and the Origin of Species', 1937); Ernst Mayr (biological species concept); G.G. Simpson (paleontology). This synthesis explained how genetic variation provides raw material for natural selection.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The 'molecular clock' hypothesis in evolutionary biology proposes that:
options: Mutations accumulate at random rates that can't be predicted
Substitutions of neutral mutations accumulate at a roughly constant rate over time, allowing time-since-divergence estimates between species from genetic differences
Mutations only occur at midnight in cells
Evolution doesn't follow any predictable timing
questions.explanation: The molecular clock (Zuckerkandl & Pauling, 1962) proposes that neutral mutations (not subject to selection) accumulate at a relatively constant rate over time. By counting genetic differences between two species and calibrating with the known fossil record, biologists estimate when species diverged. Example: humans and chimps differ in ~1.2% of their DNA → divergence ~6-7 million years ago. The clock varies between gene regions and lineages but is broadly useful.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Sickle cell anaemia provides a famous example of 'heterozygous advantage' (balanced polymorphism). Why has the disease-causing allele persisted in malaria-endemic regions of Africa despite causing severe disease in homozygotes?
options: Random genetic drift maintains the allele frequency by chance

Heterozygotes (HbA/HbS) have sickle-cell trait but are more resistant to severe malaria than HbA/HbA homozygotes, so the heterozygote has a fitness advantage that maintains the HbS allele in the population
The allele provides immunity to all infectious diseases
Modern medicine prevents the allele from being eliminated
questions.explanation: Heterozygous advantage (overdominance): Carriers (HbA/HbS) have mild sickle-cell trait but their red blood cells are inhospitable to Plasmodium falciparum, the malaria parasite — giving them substantial resistance to severe malaria. In malaria-endemic regions, heterozygote advantage outweighs the cost of having affected (HbS/HbS) children, so the HbS allele remains at ~10% frequency. This is balanced polymorphism — natural selection maintaining genetic variation rather than eliminating it.
